newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Southeast power edges higher on TVA outage.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Southeast power edges higher on TVA outage.

text.p: Spot bulk electricity prices in the U.S. Southeast were steady to slightly higher Thursday, boosted by an unexpected nuclear outage but still pressured by mild temperatures in the region.
Temperatures in the Southeast are expected to remain above-normal Friday despite a cold front moving toward the East Coast. Warmer temperatures are forecast for the region next week.

Firm, peak power into the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) territory for Friday traded in the $15.00-17.50 per megawatt hour (MWh) range, as compared with Wednesday's range of $14.00-17.00. Traders said most deals were done around $16.
Firm, off-peak power into TVA was still talked at $13.50-14.00.

Fueling the higher prices was news that TVA's 1,170 megawatt (MW) Watts Bar nuclear power unit, in Spring City, Tenn., tripped off line. The company could not comment on a restart date until after completing an investigation into the unscheduled outage.
At the Georgia/Florida border, firm, peak electricity prices in 16 hour blocks for Friday delivery were flat to higher in the $20.50-21.50 per MWh range.
Firm, off-peak power for Friday at the Ga./Fla. border was still assessed at $14.00 per MWh.
Duke Power's 846 MW Oconee 2 nuclear unit, shut since last September after a steam pipe burst, is expected to resume power output this weekend.
Oconee units 1 and 3, shut since October and each generating 846 MW, are expected to restart in February.
All three units are in Seneca, S.C.
Also, Florida Power and Light's 839 MW St Lucie 2 nuclear power unit remained at 90 percent power for inspections, but most traders agreed the power reduction was still not impacting the market.
Despite supported power prices, natural gas prices along the Gulf Coast pipes fell by five to 10 cents to the $2.91-2.96 per million British thermal units area.
